segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as set forth by [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, whom he calls Kṛṣṇācārya, delighted with [innate joy]{sahajananda} (cp.40.m1).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas tshim pa'i nag po glu dbyangs zhabs rab tu dga' bas gsungs so, 'Kāṇha of the songs (nag po glu dbyangs zhabs), satisfied by innate joy, spoke with great delight'. It renders muditaḥ as tshim pa ('satisfied') and adds rab tu dga' bas ('with great delight'). The sense is unchanged.

segments.translit: jo maṇa ityādi| mana indriy[ā]śvasya gocaro yaḥ sakalavikalpajālaḥ|| āgamamantraśāstrādijñānaṃ vā tat sarvvañca| tathāca| āgama veapurāṇetyādi|
segments.translation: “Whatever lies in the [range of the mind]{manogocara}” and so on: whatever is the range of the horse of mind and [senses]{indriya} is the net of all [conceptual thoughts]{vikalpa}. Or else the knowledge of [scripture]{agama}, [mantra]{mantra}, treatises and the like: all of that as well. And so: “[Scripture]{agama}, [Veda]{tx-veda}, [Purāṇa]{tx-purana}…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads whatever lies in the range of the mind, the range of the horse of mind and senses, as the net of all concepts, putting this where the song has [ālā jālā]{ala-jala}. He adds the knowledge of scripture, mantra, treatises and the like, and cites a verse beginning “scripture, Veda, Purāṇa” (cp.40.m2).

citations.work: Not named by Munidatta. Perhaps the dohās of Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya, Dohākoṣa), which have a couplet opening āgama-vea-purāṇe; the identification is a guess.

flags.note: Munidatta (cp.40.m2) gives no explicit gloss of ālā jālā. His paraphrase of 1a puts 'the net of all concepts' (sakalavikalpajāla) where the song has ālā jālā, perhaps hearing jāla, 'net', in jālā. Because it is a substitution, not an 'X means Y' gloss, I have not listed it under equations. The Tibetan line has mig 'phrul 'dra, 'like a magic show', for ālā jālā.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rtog pa dang rnam par rtog pa'i dra ba, 'the net of conception and concept', as though its text read kalpavikalpa- (or sakalpavikalpa-) where Shastri prints sakalavikalpa-, 'all concepts'. I translate the Sanskrit.

mana indriy[ā]śvasya: the ā is Shastri's restoration and gives aśva, 'horse' (the senses as horses is a familiar image). The Tibetan, yid dang dbang po'i spyod yul, 'the range of mind and senses', has no horse, so its text may have lacked aśva. mana-indriya could also be the single 'mind-sense', as the ala-jala entry takes it; the Tibetan dang ('and') favours 'mind and senses', which I follow.

The Tibetan has lung dang rig byed rnying ma for āgama vea purāṇe: rnying ma ('old') may render Purāṇa as a third item or as an adjective, 'the ancient Veda'. It also renders vā ('or') as yang ('also'), so that the knowledge of scripture, mantra and treatises is added rather than offered as an alternative reading of the line.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena sahajadaurllabhyaṃ pratipādayati—
ataeva vedaḥ kathaṃ sahajamanuttarajñāna[ṃ] vaktuṃ śakyate| pṛthakjanānāṃ kāyavākcittaṃ yasmin sahaje nāntarbhavati|
tathāca tilopādaḥ—
sasaṃ[58]veaṇa tantaphala tilopāe bhaṇanti|
jo maṇa goara goiyā so paramathe na honti||
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he sets forth how hard the [innate]{sahaja} is to attain:
Therefore, say: how can the [innate]{sahaja}, the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [knowledge]{jnana}, be spoken, the [innate]{sahaja} in which the [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta} of [ordinary people]{prthagjana} are not contained?
And so [Tilopāda]{p-tilopa} says:
“[Self-awareness]{svasamvedana} is the [fruit]{phala} of the [tantra]{tantra}, says [Tilopāda]{p-tilopa};
what lies hidden in the [range of the mind]{manogocara} is not the [ultimate]{paramartha}.”
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as showing how hard the innate is to attain: it is unsurpassed knowledge, which cannot be spoken, and the body, speech and mind of ordinary people are not contained in it. He quotes Tilopāda: self-awareness is the fruit of the tantra; what lies hidden in the mind's range is not the ultimate (cp.40.m3).

equations.en: the unsurpassed knowledge (anuttarajñāna), set in apposition

citations.quoted: sasaṃveaṇa tantaphala tilopāe bhaṇanti| jo maṇa goara goiyā so paramathe na honti|| (“Self-awareness is the fruit of the tantra, says Tilopāda; what lies hidden in the range of the mind is not the ultimate.”)
citations.work: An Apabhraṃśa dohā of Tilopāda, whom Munidatta names; he does not name the work (perhaps Tilopāda’s Dohākoṣa).

flags.note: Shastri prints vedaḥ, which the glossary matches as Veda (tx-veda). I read vada, 'say': a nominative vedaḥ has no construction in the sentence, while vada … kathaṃ sahajam … vaktuṃ śakyate follows the song's bhaṇa kaisẽ sahaja bola bā jāya word for word. On that reading the Veda hit is false, and I have not linked it. But the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rig byed du ji ltar … brjod par nus, 'how can it be expressed in the Veda', so its text too had a form of veda- (perhaps vede; rig byed also renders vedyo in cp.40.m4). That alternative, 'how can the innate be spoken in the Veda?', would pick up the Veda of the verse quoted in cp.40.m2.

Munidatta (cp.40.m3) says the body, speech and mind of ordinary people are not contained (nāntarbhavati) in the innate, following the song's ṇa samāya. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) drops the negative: so so'i skye bo rnams kyi lus dang ngag dang yid lhan cig skyes pa gang la thim par gyur pa, 'the innate in which the body, speech and mind of ordinary people dissolve'. Its own quotation of 2b keeps the negative (mi 'jug).
Munidatta's daurlabhya, 'being hard to attain', is smra dka' ba, 'being hard to speak of', in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): a free rendering suited to the refrain, or a different reading.

In Tilopāda's verse, tanta is most simply tantra ('the fruit of the tantra'), but it may be a slip for tatta (tattva, 'reality'); the Tibetan, so so rang rig 'bras bu ni ('individual self-awareness is the fruit'), renders neither. sasaṃveaṇa is svasaṃvedana, 'self-awareness'. I take goiyā as 'hidden' (gopita); the Tibetan sbas ('hidden') agrees. The verse's jo maṇa goara echoes the song's 1a.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena tattvasvarūpamāha—
alemityādi| alaṃ niṣpha(ska)laṃ guruḥ śiṣyāyopadeśaṃ dadāti| yo'pi sahajaḥ sa kathā vedyo na bhavati| tena guruṇā kiṃ kṛtvā vaktavyamiti|
tathāca sarahapādāḥ—
na taṃ vāe guru kahai ityādi|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [reality]{tattva}:
“In vain…” and so on. In vain (alam), meaning fruitlessly, the [guru]{guru} gives [instruction]{upadesa} to the [disciple]{sisya}. The [innate]{sahaja} cannot be known through talk. So what is the [guru]{guru} to do, to speak it?
And so the venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha}:
“The [guru]{guru} does not tell it in words…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as stating the true nature of reality. He glosses āle as fruitless: the guru instructs the disciple in vain, because the innate cannot be known through talk, so how could the guru speak it? He quotes Saraha: “the guru does not tell it in words” (cp.40.m4).

citations.quoted: na taṃ vāe guru kahai… (“The guru does not tell it in words…”)
citations.work: Saraha, probably his Dohākoṣa (Munidatta names Saraha but not the work).

flags.note: Munidatta (cp.40.m4) glosses alam as niṣphalam, 'fruitless, in vain', which the draft's 3a follows. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads it as 'false': its comment has brdzun pa zhes bya ba … bden pa ma yin pas bla mas slob ma la man ngag ster bar byed do ('“falsely” and so on: by what is not true the guru gives the disciple instruction'), matching its line 3a, brdzun gyi thabs kyis ('by false means').
niṣpha(ska)laṃ: Shastri's parenthesis offers niṣkalam ('partless') beside niṣphalam. 'Fruitless' suits alam and the couplet, and I follow it.

kathā vedyo: either kathā for kathayā ('through talk') or a compound kathāvedya ('knowable through talk'); the sense is the same. The Tibetan, rig byed ma yin ('is not knowable', the same rig byed that stands for veda- in cp.40.m3), has no word for talk.
The Tibetan of Saraha's line, de med bla mas ji ltar smra ('how can the guru speak of what is not there?'), differs from the Apabhraṃśa, 'the guru does not tell it in words'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena tamevārthaṃ dṛḍhayati—
tejai ityādi| tasmāt bhagavatī(ti) mātragatyā yadyadbhaṇyate sahajaṃ tat sarvvaṃ ṭālanamasadrūpaṃ| yo'pi vajraguruḥ so'pyasmin dharmme vacanadaridratve(rtha)na yuktaḥ| tasya śiṣyeṇāpyavacastvena kiñcinna śrutam|
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he makes that same point firm:
“So whatever…” (tejai) and so on. Therefore whatever is spoken of as the [innate]{sahaja} by way of mere speech, all of that is [ṭāla]{tala}: of unreal form. Even the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru} is poor in words in this [dharma]{dharma}. And his [disciple]{sisya}, too, has heard nothing at all, because there are no words.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as confirming the point: whatever is said of the innate in mere words is [ṭāla]{tala}, which he glosses “of unreal form”, as on song 33 (cp.33.m2). Even the vajra guru is poor in words in this dharma, and his disciple, with no words spoken, hears nothing at all (cp.40.m5).

flags.note: Munidatta (cp.40.m5) quotes 4a as tejai, not je tai as in the song. His paraphrase, tasmāt … yad yad … tat sarvaṃ ('therefore … whatever … all of that'), would suit te jai, 'so, whatever'. The lemma in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), gang de ('whatever, that'), follows the song's order. I render the lemma with the draft's opening words.

Shastri prints bhagavatī(ti) mātragatyā, 'the Blessed Lady (thus) by way of mere…', which makes no sense here. I read bhaṇitimātragatyā, 'by way of mere speech'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de las byung ba'i tshig tsam du gyur pa ('become mere words arisen from that'): tshig tsam ('mere words') supports -mātra with a word for speech, and byung ba / gyur pa suggest its text had a form of bhavati. It is not the Blessed Lady (p-bhagavati), and I have not linked it.

ṭālanam is Munidatta's Sanskritized form of the song's ṭāla; I give it the glossary's ṭāla. He glosses it asadrūpa, 'of unreal form', as on song 33, where (per the glossary) he explains ṭā as ṭamāla, 'the unreal form' (cp.33.m2). The Tibetan has brdzun te rang bzhin bden pa ma yin pa ('false: its nature is not true'), matching brdzun in its line 4a.

Munidatta (cp.40.m5) says the vajra guru is 'poor in words' (vacanadaridratvena yuktaḥ) and that the disciple heard nothing because there are no words. That fits the draft's emended 4b, 'the guru is mute, the disciple deaf', but does not prove it: 'poor in words' is a paraphrase, not the word boba or mūka, and he gives no gloss of bodha, the transmitted reading. The Tibetan comment agrees (tshig gis phongs, 'poor in words'), but its line 4b, bla ma'i thabs kyis slob ma 'khrul bar byas ('by the guru's means the disciple was confused'), seems to read guru-bodha, not 'mute'. And in cp.40.m6 his simile makes the guru the deaf one.

The Tibetan renders yuktaḥ as rigs pa ('it is fitting' that the guru is poor in words), and has tshig nyid kyis ('through words themselves') where the Sanskrit has avacastvena ('because there are no words'), without the negative. Shastri's parenthetical (rtha) in vacanadaridratve(rtha)na is unclear; 'poverty of words' stands either way.

segments.translit:
ataeva so'pi ca badhirastasmin gambhīradharmme matiṃ pratipādayati—
bhaṇai ityādi| kṛṣṇācāryyo hi vadati| kīdṛśaṃ jinaratnaṃ ratimanantamanuttarasukhaṃ tanotīti ratnaṃ caturthānandaṃ boddhavyaṃ| yathā badhiraḥ saṃketādinā mūkasya saṃbodhanaṃ [58ka] karoti tadvaddūre sadguruḥ śiṣye ratisvaprabhāveṇa mahāsukhaṃ tanoti|
tathāca iuḍīpādāḥ|
adūre dūre vetyādi|| 40||
segments.translation:
Hence he too, deaf as he is, imparts [intelligence]{mati} of that profound [dharma]{dharma}:
“[Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says” and so on: that is, [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says. What is the [Jina]{p-jina}’s [jewel]{ratna} like? It spreads delight, endless, [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [bliss]{sukha}; so it is a [jewel]{ratna}, to be understood as the fourth [joy]{ananda}. Just as a [deaf]{badhira} man instructs a [mute]{muka} by signs and the like, so the true [guru]{guru}, from afar, spreads [great bliss]{mahasukha} in the [disciple]{sisya} by the [power]{prabhava} of his own delight.
And so the venerable [Iuṛīpāda]{p-iuri}:
“Near or far…” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the Jina's jewel as the fourth joy, which spreads endless, unsurpassed bliss. His simile pairs the deaf one with the true guru and the mute with the disciple: as a deaf man gets through to a mute by signs, so the true guru, from afar, spreads great bliss in the disciple by the power of delight (cp.40.m6).

citations.work: Iuṛīpāda, whom Munidatta names; the work is unidentified.

flags.note: The opening (cp.40.m6), ataeva so 'pi ca badhiras tasmin gambhīradharme matiṃ pratipādayati, can be one sentence, 'hence he too, deaf, imparts understanding of that profound dharma', which I follow; or 'Hence he too is deaf', then Munidatta's usual framing, '[the poet] sets forth understanding of that profound dharma'. 'He too' is most likely the guru: the disciple was deaf in 4b, and in the simile the deaf one is the true guru. The Tibetan, de yang 'on pa ste der zab mo'i chos la blo gros rtogs pa'o, has rtogs pa, 'understands', for pratipādayati.

In Munidatta's simile (cp.40.m6) the deaf man instructs the mute, as in the song's 5b, and the deaf one stands for the true guru, the mute for the disciple. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reverses the roles: dper na 'on pa la brda la sogs pas lkugs pa'i rtogs pa smra bar byed do ('by signs and the like the mute's understanding is told to the deaf'), matching its line 5b, lkugs pas 'on par smra ba ('as the mute speaks to the deaf'). The correspondence comes from the simile (yathā … tadvat), not an explicit gloss, so it is not under equations.

ratim … tanotīti ratnam is probably an etymology: it is a ratna because it spreads (tanoti) delight (rati). The Tibetan … phyir ('because') also takes it causally. 'Delight' renders rati here and in ratisvaprabhāveṇa; it is not the glossary's 'delight' (ullāsa). svaprabhāva may be the guru's own power or delight's own power; dūre ('from afar') probably anticipates the quotation adūre dūre vā ('near or far').

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rin po che bzhi po'i dga' ba ('the joy of the four …') for caturthānanda, probably for bzhi pa'i ('fourth'); it renders tanoti as rgya chen po / rgya cher ('vast, extensively'), and ratisvaprabhāveṇa as dga' ba'i mthus ('by the power of joy'), without 'own'. It names the quoted teacher Da u Da'i zhabs and quotes ring ba ma yin ring ba ('not far, far') for adūre dūre.

questions: Munidatta names the poet Kṛṣṇācārya (cp.40.m1, cp.40.m6), but the glossary gives only “Kāṇha” for p-kanha, so I used that. Should Kṛṣṇācārya be a listed variant for the commentary?

cp.40.m3: do you accept vada (“say”, glossing the song’s bhaṇa) for the printed vedaḥ? The Tibetan rig byed du (“in the Veda”) shows that its text also had veda-. If you accept it, the tx-veda match on বেদঃ should be suppressed for this segment.
3a: the draft follows Munidatta’s niṣphalam, “in vain” (cp.40.m4); the Tibetan line and comment have “false” (brdzun). Keep “In vain”, or add “falsely” as an alternative in a note on the line?

4b: Munidatta’s “poor in words” (cp.40.m5) fits the emendation “the guru is mute” but does not attest boba, and the Tibetan line reads “by the guru’s means” (bla ma’i thabs kyis). Keep the emendation in the line, or translate the transmitted reading and give the emendation in a note?

5b: Munidatta’s simile (cp.40.m6) makes the deaf one the true guru, while the emended 4b makes the guru mute; the Tibetan keeps the guru on the mute side in both places. Should the note on 5b point out this swap of roles?

cp.40.m6: I used the approved “intelligence” for mati (“imparts intelligence of that profound dharma”); “understanding” reads better here. rati (“delight”, twice in cp.40.m6) has no entry and collides in English with ullāsa, “delight”: do you want an entry for it?
